claim: Trans-species small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are delivered to host plants from diverse pathogens and parasites.
source: Trans-species small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are delivered to host plants from diverse pathogens and parasites and can target host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on fungal pathogens, oomycetes, and parasitic plants in the Introduction section.

claim: Trans-species sRNAs can target host mRNAs.
source: Trans-species small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are delivered to host plants from diverse pathogens and parasites and can target host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multiple species of the parasitic plant Cuscuta produce trans-species sRNAs that collectively target many host mRNAs.
source: Multiple species of the parasitic plant Cuscuta produce trans-species sRNAs that collectively target many host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from four Cuscuta species showing HI-sRNAs and confirmed targets.

claim: Confirmed target sites are nearly always in highly conserved, protein-coding regions of host mRNAs.
source: Confirmed target sites are nearly always in highly conserved, protein-coding regions of host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 5C and alignment data.

claim: Cuscuta trans-species sRNAs can be grouped into superfamilies that have variation in a three-nucleotide period.
source: Cuscuta trans-species sRNAs can be grouped into superfamilies that have variation in a three-nucleotide period.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis and sequence alignments shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Superfamily variants compensate for synonymous-site variation in host mRNAs.
source: These variants compensate for synonymous-site variation in host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing significant co-variation between sRNA superfamilies and target sites.

claim: Fungal plant pathogens produce sRNAs with complementarity to host mRNAs.
source: Fungal plant pathogens produce sRNAs with complementarity to host mRNAs (Weiberg et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiberg et al., 2013.

claim: Host plants produce trans-species sRNAs that silence mRNAs in pathogenic fungi.
source: host plants produce trans-species sRNAs that silence mRNAs in both pathogenic fungi (Zhang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2016 and Cai et al., 2018.

claim: Host plants produce trans-species sRNAs that silence mRNAs in oomycetes.
source: host plants produce trans-species sRNAs that silence mRNAs in both pathogenic fungi (Zhang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2018) and oomycetes (Hou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hou et al., 2019.

claim: The parasitic plant Cuscuta campestris produces trans-species microRNAs (miRNAs) which silence mRNAs in multiple host plants.
source: The parasitic plant Cuscuta campestris produces trans-species microRNAs (miRNAs) which silence mRNAs in multiple host plants (Shahid et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahid et al., 2018.

claim: Silencing by plant trans-species sRNAs relies on extensive complementarity between the sRNA and target mRNA, similar to normal endogenous plant miRNAs.
source: Silencing by plant trans-species sRNAs relies on extensive complementarity between the sRNA and target mRNA, similar to normal endogenous plant miRNAs (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Trans-species silencing is expected to benefit the source organism while being detrimental to the target organism in parasitic/pathogenic relationships.
source: Trans-species silencing is expected to benefit the source organism while being detrimental to the target organism in parasitic/pathogenic relationships.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the nature of parasitic/pathogenic relationships.

claim: Target sites are not under purifying selection to maintain complementarity to trans-species sRNAs.
source: This implies that target sites are not under purifying selection to maintain complementarity to trans-species sRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the expectation that trans-species silencing is detrimental to the target organism.

claim: MiRNAs are defined by the precise excision of a single mature, functional small RNA.
source: MiRNAs are defined by the precise excision of a single mature, functional small RNA (Axtell and Meyers, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Axtell and Meyers, 2018.

claim: The precise excision of miRNAs implies selection for the miRNA to target a particular sequence or closely related set of sequences.
source: MiRNAs are defined by the precise excision of a single mature, functional small RNA (Axtell and Meyers, 2018), which implies selection for the miRNA to target a particular sequence or closely related set of sequences.
evidence: Inferred from the definition of miRNAs.

claim: All four Cuscuta species studied are generalists with documented hosts spanning multiple plant families.
source: All four Cuscuta species are generalists with documented hosts spanning multiple plant families (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by herbaria data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several hundred Cuscuta sRNAs in each experiment were significantly up-regulated in the interface tissue relative to parasite stems (FDR < 0.1).
source: Differential expression analysis revealed several hundred Cuscuta sRNAs in each experiment that were significantly up-regulated in the interface tissue relative to parasite stems (FDR < 0.1) (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: Supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis.

claim: HI-sRNAs are mostly 21 or 22 nucleotides long.
source: HI-sRNAs are mostly 21 or 22 nucleotides long (Figure 1A)
evidence: Shown in size distribution plots in Figure 1A.

claim: 21 or 22 nucleotide sizes are consistent with either miRNAs or short interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
source: HI-sRNAs are mostly 21 or 22 nucleotides long (Figure 1A), sizes consistent with either miRNAs or short interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sRNA sizes.

claim: Distinguishing miRNAs from siRNAs requires a genome assembly.
source: Distinguishing miRNAs from siRNAs requires a genome assembly (Axtell and Meyers, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Axtell and Meyers, 2018.

claim: Approximately half of the C. campestris HI-sRNAs (208/408) come from MIRNA hairpins.
source: Approximately half of the C. campestris HI-sRNAs (208/408) come from MIRNA hairpins (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by annotation analysis using the C. campestris genome.

claim: C. campestris-derived HI-sRNAs were recovered from 40 of the 42 novel MIRNA loci described by Shahid et al. (2018).
source: C. campestris-derived HI-sRNAs were recovered from 40 of the 42 novel MIRNA loci described by Shahid et al. (2018)
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously published MIRNA annotations.

claim: Representatives from all five miRNA families previously demonstrated to target host mRNAs were recovered.
source: C. campestris-derived HI-sRNAs were recovered from 40 of the 42 novel MIRNA loci described by Shahid et al. (2018), including representatives from all five miRNA families previously demonstrated to target host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously published data.

claim: When using a strict cutoff (maximum edit distance of 1), the majority of HI-sRNAs were not observed in more than one species.
source: Surprisingly, when using a strict cutoff (maximum edit distance of 1) we found that the majority of HI-sRNAs were not observed in more than one species (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C family grouping analysis.

claim: In many cases HI-sRNAs were unique to single isolates of a single species.
source: In many cases HI-sRNAs were unique to single isolates of a single species (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C family grouping analysis.

claim: HI-sRNAs could be rapidly differentiating in expression, sequence, or both within these Cuscuta species.
source: This result implies that HI-sRNAs could be rapidly differentiating in expression, sequence, or both within these Cuscuta species.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that most HI-sRNAs are not conserved between species or isolates.

claim: C. campestris HI-sRNAs can target host mRNAs in several hosts.
source: Our previous work showed that C. campestris HI-sRNAs can target host mRNAs in several hosts (Shahid et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahid et al., 2018.

claim: Secondary siRNAs can accumulate from mRNAs as a result of an initial miRNA- or siRNA-directed targeting event, especially when the initiating sRNA is 22 nucleotides long.
source: Secondary siRNAs can accumulate from mRNAs as a result of an initial miRNA- or siRNA-directed targeting event, especially when the initiating sRNA is 22 nucleotides long (Cuperus et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cuperus et al., 2010.

claim: A large portion of HI-sRNAs are 22-nt or are clustered from some sRNAs which are 22-nt in length.
source: A large portion of HI-sRNAs are 22-nt or are clustered from some sRNAs which are 22-nt in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A. thaliana xrn4 mutants over-accumulate 5' remnants of sRNA-mediated mRNA cleavage.
source: A. thaliana xrn4 mutants were used as hosts for these experiments because they over-accumulate 5' remnants of sRNA-mediated mRNA cleavage (Rymarquis et al., 2011; Schon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rymarquis et al., 2011 and Schon et al., 2018.

claim: The CRCK2 mRNA is targeted by a C. pentagona HI-sRNA with both degradome and secondary siRNA evidence.
source: The CRCK2 mRNA is an example with both degradome and secondary siRNA evidence of targeting by a C. pentagona HI-sRNA (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A-E with target prediction, secondary siRNA accumulation, and NanoPARE data.

claim: 61 target sites over 54 A. thaliana mRNAs are targeted by Cuscuta HI-sRNAs confirmed by a single method.
source: Altogether these two analyses yielded a set of 61 target sites over 54 A. thaliana mRNAs targeted by Cuscuta HI-sRNAs confirmed by a single method
evidence: Supported by degradome and secondary siRNA analysis.

claim: Seven target sites are confirmed by both degradome and secondary siRNA methods.
source: Altogether these two analyses yielded a set of 61 target sites over 54 A. thaliana mRNAs targeted by Cuscuta HI-sRNAs confirmed by a single method and seven more confirmed by both (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Accumulation of confirmed target mRNAs is generally down-regulated in parasitized host stems.
source: Based on RNA-seq analysis, accumulation of confirmed target mRNAs is generally down-regulated in parasitized host stems (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in cumulative density plots in Figure 3.

claim: This work greatly expands on the set of six mRNAs previously identified as host targets of C. campestris miRNAs.
source: This greatly expands on the set of six mRNAs previously identified as host targets of C. campestris miRNAs (Shahid et al., 2018)
evidence: Comparison with previously published data.

claim: Trans-species sRNAs are used by multiple Cuscuta species.
source: This greatly expands on the set of six mRNAs previously identified as host targets of C. campestris miRNAs (Shahid et al., 2018), and demonstrates that trans-species sRNAs are used by multiple Cuscuta species.
evidence: Supported by confirmed targets from four different Cuscuta species.

claim: C. campestris homologs of targeted A. thaliana mRNAs invariably have lower complementarity to HI-sRNAs.
source: Target predictions show that C. campestris homologs of targeted A. thaliana mRNAs invariably have lower complementarity to HI-sRNAs (Figure 4).
evidence: Shown in target prediction score comparison in Figure 4.

claim: Only four confirmed targeting interactions were found for C. campestris mRNAs by HI-sRNAs.
source: Repeating the analysis pipeline to examine possible self-targeting of C. campestris mRNAs by HI-sRNAs found only four confirmed targeting interactions
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HI-sRNAs may largely function in trans in the host.
source: Repeating the analysis pipeline to examine possible self-targeting of C. campestris mRNAs by HI-sRNAs found only four confirmed targeting interactions, an indication that HI-sRNAs may largely function in trans in the host (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the low number of self-targeting interactions compared to host targeting.

claim: SEOR1 is the most frequently targeted mRNA by HI-sRNAs from multiple species.
source: Some mRNAs were confirmed to be targeted by HI-sRNAs from multiple species, with the most frequent interaction being with SEOR1 (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SEOR1 encodes a phloem protein that acts to reduce sap loss after wounding.
source: SEOR1 encodes a phloem protein that acts to reduce sap loss after wounding (Knoblauch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knoblauch et al., 2014.

claim: C. campestris growth is enhanced when A. thaliana seor1 mutants are used as hosts.
source: C. campestris growth is enhanced when A. thaliana seor1 mutants are used as hosts (Shahid et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahid et al., 2018.

claim: The majority of mRNAs confirmed as targets are unique to a single Cuscuta species or isolate.
source: However, the majority of mRNAs confirmed as targets are unique to a single Cuscuta species or isolate (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The current analysis is likely to have missed many targets due to lack of sensitivity of the methods.
source: Additionally, our current analysis is likely to have missed many targets, both due to lack of sensitivity of our methods (secondary siRNA accumulation and/or degradome analysis both can miss true targets)
evidence: Based on known limitations of the methods used.

claim: A. thaliana is unlikely to be a major host of Cuscuta in nature.
source: Additionally, our current analysis is likely to have missed many targets, both due to lack of sensitivity of our methods (secondary siRNA accumulation and/or degradome analysis both can miss true targets), and because A. thaliana is unlikely to be a major host of Cuscuta in nature.
evidence: Inferred from herbaria data showing Cuscuta species parasitize diverse plant families.

claim: Genes involved in auxin signaling repeatedly appear as targets.
source: Genes involved in auxin signaling repeatedly appear, including the previously identified targets TIR1, AFB2, and AFB3 (Shahid et al., 2018) and new targets PXY (Etchells et al., 2012) and ARK2 (Sankaranarayanan and Samuel, 2015) with a proposed role in auxin response.
evidence: Supported by confirmed targeting data and citations.

claim: Auxin signaling is potentially connected to defense against Cuscuta through its role in glucosinolate production.
source: Auxin signaling is involved in many processes in the plant, and is potentially connected to defense against Cuscuta through its role in glucosinolate production (Smith et al., 2016; Salehin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016 and Salehin et al., 2019.

claim: Phloem protein mRNAs are targeted, including OPS and SEOR1.
source: Phloem protein mRNAs are targeted, adding OPS (Truernit et al., 2012) to the previously identified SEOR1.
evidence: Supported by confirmed targeting data and citations.

claim: A receptor-like kinase (CuRe1) from tomato is a resistance gene that prevents Cuscuta reflexa infestation.
source: A receptor-like kinase (CuRe1) from tomato is a resistance gene that prevents Cuscuta reflexa infestation (Hegenauer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hegenauer et al., 2016.

claim: Receptor-like kinases and kinases in general are well represented in the set of HI-sRNA targets.
source: Receptor-like kinases and kinases in general are well represented in the set of HI-sRNA targets, including several that are involved in defense responses.
evidence: Supported by confirmed targeting data.

claim: MPK3 is a well-known defense regulator.
source: This includes the well-known defense regulator MPK3 (Asai et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Asai et al., 2002.

claim: BIK1 is involved in defense responses.
source: This includes the well-known defense regulator MPK3 (Asai et al., 2002) and previously discovered BIK1 (Veronese et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veronese et al., 2006.

claim: Brassinosteroid (BR) signaling pathway is targeted, with targets BRI1, MAPKKK5, and PICKLE.
source: Another targeted pathway is brassinosteroid (BR) signaling, with targets BRI1 (Planas-Riverola et al., 2019), MAPKKK5 (Yan et al., 2018), and PICKLE (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by confirmed targeting data and citations.

claim: BR has a clear role in defense, with connections to both BIK1 and MPK3.
source: BR has a clear role in defense, with connections to both BIK1 and MPK3 (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: An overall theme of targeting host immunity and vascular system function emerges from the set of confirmed targets.
source: An overall theme of targeting host immunity and vascular system function emerges from this set of confirmed targets.
evidence: Inferred from the functional categories of confirmed target genes.

claim: Plant miRNAs that initially seem unrelated based on divergent sequences can sometimes be grouped into superfamilies.
source: Plant miRNAs that initially seem unrelated based on divergent sequences can sometimes be grouped into superfamilies (Xia et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xia et al., 2013.

claim: Many superfamilies of Cuscuta HI-sRNAs were found, with a substantial portion shared between species and isolates.
source: Many superfamilies of Cuscuta HI-sRNAs were found, with a substantial portion of them shared between species and isolates (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A superfamily grouping analysis.

claim: 19 superfamilies were shared between all isolates except C. indecora.
source: 19 superfamilies were shared between all isolates except C. indecora
evidence: Supported by superfamily clustering analysis.

claim: 14 superfamilies were present in at least one isolate each of C. campestris, C. pentagona, and C. gronovii.
source: 19 superfamilies were shared between all isolates except C. indecora, and another 14 superfamilies were present in at least one isolate each of C. campestris, C. pentagona, and C. gronovii.
evidence: Supported by superfamily clustering analysis.

claim: 158 out of 332 superfamilies which contain C. campestris HI-sRNAs are likely miRNAs.
source: Leveraging the prior C. campestris miRNA annotations, we can extrapolate that 158 out of 332 superfamilies which contain C. campestris HI-sRNAs are likely miRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with C. campestris MIRNA annotations.

claim: Of the superfamilies present in C. campestris with proven target relationships, 22 out of 23 are likely to be miRNAs.
source: Furthermore, we extrapolate that of the superfamilies present in C. campestris with proven target relationships, 22 out of 23 are likely to be miRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with C. campestris MIRNA annotations.

claim: HI-sRNAs within a superfamily vary at several positions both between and within species.
source: HI-sRNAs within a superfamily vary at several positions both between and within species (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in sequence alignments in Figure 5B.

claim: In many cases variation within superfamilies occurred in a visible three-nucleotide period.
source: In many cases variation within superfamilies occurred in a visible three-nucleotide period (e.g. SupFam_24, SupFam_37; Figure 5B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Shown in sequence alignments in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: HI-sRNAs target highly-conserved protein-coding positions.
source: Analysis of translated target site conservation shows that HI-sRNAs target highly-conserved protein-coding positions (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in conservation analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Positional variations in HI-sRNA superfamilies precisely correspond to variable positions in homologous target sequences.
source: Positional variations in HI-sRNA superfamilies precisely correspond to variable positions in homologous target sequences (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in aligned sequences in Figure 5B.

claim: Variation is frequently apparent at synonymous sites, accounting for the three-nucleotide periodicity of superfamily variation.
source: This variation is frequently apparent at synonymous sites, accounting for the three-nucleotide periodicity of superfamily variation.
evidence: Inferred from the alignment of sRNA superfamilies with target sites showing codon-level variation.

claim: 18 significant (p-value<0.05, Pearson correlation) examples of co-variation between HI-sRNA superfamilies and eudicot target sites were found.
source: Modeling correlation of positional variation between HI-sRNA superfamilies and eudicot target sites found 18 significant (p-value<0.05, Pearson correlation) examples of this type of co-variation (Supplementary file 7, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: HI-sRNA superfamily variation occurs within single Cuscuta species.
source: Importantly, HI-sRNA superfamily variation occurs within single Cuscuta species (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 7)
evidence: Shown in sequence alignments in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Multiple HI-sRNA variants are commonly deployed by a given parasite during infestation.
source: Importantly, HI-sRNA superfamily variation occurs within single Cuscuta species (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 7), such that multiple HI-sRNA variants are commonly deployed by a given parasite during infestation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that superfamily variation occurs within single species.

claim: By targeting conserved sites and making several HI-sRNA variants that collectively cover many/most possible synonymous target variants, Cuscuta may ensure successful targeting across a wide range of hosts.
source: By targeting conserved sites, and making several HI-sRNA variants that collectively cover many/most possible synonymous target variants, Cuscuta may ensure successful targeting across a wide range of hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the observed patterns of sRNA variation and target site conservation.

claim: Evidence of targeting was found in transcripts homologous to known A. thaliana targets in N. benthamiana.
source: Using sRNA-seq libraries made from C. campestris attachments on Nicotiana benthamiana (Shahid et al., 2018), we found evidence of targeting in transcripts homologous to known A. thaliana targets (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sRNA-seq data from C. campestris on N. benthamiana.

claim: N. benthamiana target mRNAs were generally down-regulated in interface tissues.
source: Additionally, N. benthamiana target mRNAs were generally down-regulated in interface tissues (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 10.
evidence: Shown in qRT-PCR data in Figure 6A.

claim: The N. benthamiana TIR1 target sites encode identical amino acids, but vary at synonymous positions.
source: The N. benthamiana TIR1 target sites encode identical amino acids, but vary at synonymous positions.
evidence: Shown in sequence alignments in Figure 6B.

claim: Some SupFam_27 variants are more complementary than others to different TIR1 homologs.
source: Some SupFam_27 variants are more complementary than others from each of the different homologs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown in complementarity score heatmap in Figure 6B.

claim: Variation in a Cuscuta sRNA superfamily accommodates synonymous-site variation in confirmed target mRNAs from different plant species.
source: This provides a direct example where variation in a Cuscuta sRNA superfamily accommodates synonymous-site variation in confirmed target mRNAs from different plant species.
evidence: Demonstrated by the TIR1 targeting example in Figure 6B.

claim: Ten examples of gene family-specific motifs potentially targeted by Cuscuta HI-sRNA superfamilies were found within A. thaliana.
source: We examined target predictions within A. thaliana and found ten examples of gene family-specific motifs potentially targeted by Cuscuta HI-sRNA superfamilies (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: Supported by target prediction analysis within A. thaliana.

claim: A HI-sRNA superfamily is predicted to target the mRNA region encoding the WRKY motifs within the WRKY family of defense-related transcription factors.
source: These include a HI-sRNA superfamily predicted to target the mRNA region encoding the eponymous WRKY motifs within the well-known family of defense-related transcription factors (Pandey and Somssich, 2009).
evidence: Supported by target prediction analysis and citation.

claim: Multiple Cuscuta species use trans-species HI-sRNAs to target a substantial number of host mRNAs.
source: We conclude that multiple Cuscuta species use trans-species HI-sRNAs to target a substantial number of host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by confirmed targeting data from four Cuscuta species.

claim: Many if not most of these HI-siRNAs are likely to be miRNAs.
source: Many if not most of these HI-siRNAs are likely to be miRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from C. campestris genome annotation showing ~50% of HI-sRNAs come from MIRNA hairpins.

claim: Host genes involved in pathogen defense, hormone signaling, and vascular system function are common targets of Cuscuta trans-species HI-sRNAs.
source: Host genes involved in pathogen defense, hormone signaling, and vascular system function are common targets of Cuscuta trans-species HI-sRNAs.
evidence: Supported by functional analysis of confirmed target genes.

claim: Cuscuta trans-species HI-sRNAs nearly always interact with highly conserved target sites within the coding sequences of host mRNAs.
source: Cuscuta trans-species HI-sRNAs nearly always interact with highly conserved target sites within the coding sequences of host mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HI-sRNAs can often be grouped into superfamilies that have nucleotide diversity that corresponds with target site variation primarily at synonymous sites.
source: HI-sRNAs can often be grouped into superfamilies that have nucleotide diversity that corresponds with target site variation primarily at synonymous sites.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and sequence alignments.

claim: Host target sites are likely under purifying selection because they code for critical amino acids that have little variation even among distantly related eudicots.
source: It seems likely that host target sites are under purifying selection because they code for critical amino acids that have little variation even among distantly related eudicots.
evidence: Inferred from conservation analysis of target sites across 36 eudicot species.

claim: By targeting constrained protein-coding sites and deploying an array of sRNA variants that cover most possible permutations of synonymous site variation, Cuscuta HI-sRNAs are likely to be robust against the evolution of host resistance by target site sequence changes.
source: By targeting these already constrained protein-coding sites, and deploying an array of sRNA variants that cover most possible permutations of synonymous site variation, Cuscuta HI-sRNAs are likely to be robust against the evolution of host resistance by target site sequence changes.
evidence: Inferred from the observed patterns of targeting and variation.

claim: The strategy used by Cuscuta is suitable for a generalist parasite that interacts with diverse hosts.
source: This is also a suitable strategy for a generalist parasite that interacts with diverse hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all four Cuscuta species are generalists and the targeting strategy accommodates host diversity.

claim: The strategy used by Cuscuta provides a novel paradigm for the molecular evolution of trans-species sRNA targeting during parasitism.
source: The strategy used by Cuscuta provides a novel paradigm for the molecular evolution of trans-species sRNA targeting during parasitism.
evidence: Inferred from the unique characteristics of the Cuscuta trans-species sRNA system.
